summary: I reviewed the dvpwa (aiohttp) application: all DAO modules, views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, app bootstrap, Jinja2 setup and templates, services (db/redis) and config. The app is highly vulnerable: an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create allows full DB compromise, and disabled autoescaping produces stored XSS. CSRF protection is disabled, session cookies are not HttpOnly, and passwords use unsalted MD5. Static assets (materialize/jquery) were not audited.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT query by Python %-formatting the user-supplied name directly into the SQL string, instead of passing it as a bound parameter (as every other DAO does). The POST /students/ handler (sqli/views.py:54-57) calls Student.create(conn, data['name']) with the raw form field and, unlike other write handlers, has no @authorize decorator, so any unauthenticated visitor can inject SQL. A name such as "x'); DROP TABLE students;--" or a value with a single quote breaks out of the string literal, enabling arbitrary SQL (data exfiltration via stacked/boolean queries, modification, or reading the users table with password hashes). This is the primary, fully reachable vulnerability of the app.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  ->  cur.execute(q). Source: views.students POST -> data['name'] (unauthenticated route in routes.py:14).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query like the other DAOs: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with % / f-strings from user input.

findings.title: Stored XSS via globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables render raw HTML by default. User-controlled data is emitted without escaping and persisted, producing stored XSS. The clearest sink is course review text: an attacker POSTs a review containing <script>...</script> at /courses/{id}/review (Review.create stores it verbatim), and it is rendered unescaped at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 ({{ review.review_text }}) to every visitor of the course page. The same missing escaping affects course.title/description (course.jinja2:9,14,15,32), student name (students.jinja2:16), and error fields — only a couple of spots use the explicit |e filter. Combined with non-HttpOnly session cookies (below), this allows session hijacking.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink: templates/course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` fed by Review.create (dao/review.py:28-36) from views.review data['review_text'].
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) and only mark trusted content safe explicitly.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled (csrf_middleware not registered)
findings.description: The application defines a csrf_middleware (sqli/middlewares.py:26-38) that validates a per-session _csrf_token on POST, but it is commented out of the middleware list, so no CSRF check runs. All state-changing endpoints (login, create student — which is also the SQLi sink, create course, submit review, evaluate/grade, logout) accept cross-site forged POSTs. Because tokens are never enforced, an attacker page can silently make an authenticated victim (e.g. an admin) create records, post reviews, or assign marks, and can drive the unauthenticated SQLi endpoint from a victim's browser.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware,  error_middleware]. The token-checking csrf_middleware exists but is never added.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure every POST form includes the {{ csrf_token() }} hidden field (most already do).

findings.title: Session cookie stored without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript via document.cookie. Given the stored XSS above, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack authenticated/admin sessions. No Secure flag is set either.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True (with an appropriate SameSite value) for the session cookie.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password) with no salt and no work factor. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage; if the users table is disclosed (readily possible via the SQL injection above), the unsalted digests fall to rainbow-table/brute-force attacks almost instantly, exposing plaintext passwords and enabling credential reuse.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hashing algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2) and migrate stored hashes; also use a constant-time comparison.

findings.title: Debug mode enabled in application factory
findings.description: The aiohttp Application is created with debug=True unconditionally. In production this enables verbose diagnostics/tracebacks and looser behavior that can leak internal details to clients and aid attackers. It should be controlled by configuration/environment rather than hard-coded on.
findings.recommendation: Set debug from config/environment and default it to False in production.
